record_identity.title: Oklahoma judge used ChatGPT research in order containing two nonexistent case citations

incident_identity.historical_event_name: 2025 Oklahoma Judge Wheeler ChatGPT nonexistent-citation order incident
incident_identity.date_basis: Reuters and USA Today Network reporting identify the affected paternity-case order as a 2025 order but do not establish the exact issuance date in the reviewed sources.

summary: Stephens County Associate District Judge Lawrence Wheeler acknowledged using ChatGPT for legal research in connection with a 2025 child-paternity case order that contained citations to two cases that do not exist, according to an August 17, 2026 letter from District Attorney Jason Hicks describing Wheeler's statement to the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation. Reporting identifies the nonexistent cases as Cummings v. Cimarron Elevator Co. and Hawkins v. Linhart. Wheeler said he created the order himself and used ChatGPT only for research. The order was later vacated after an attorney challenged the citations at the Oklahoma Supreme Court. The Oklahoma Attorney General's Office stated that the evidence reviewed did not support criminal prosecution; possible judicial discipline remained a separate matter.

vigil_assessment.factual_basis: Reuters reports, based on an August 17, 2026 letter from Stephens County District Attorney Jason Hicks to the Oklahoma attorney general's office, that Judge Lawrence Wheeler told an Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation investigator he used ChatGPT for research and that an order he drafted contained two citations produced by ChatGPT to cases that do not exist. USA Today Network reporting reproduced through Reuters Connect provides the same account, identifies the two fictitious case names, states that the order was issued in a 2025 child-paternity case, and reports that Wheeler later vacated the order after it was challenged.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: The material governance issue is epistemic reliance in an authoritative judicial artefact. Fictitious AI-produced case citations entered a signed court order even though the validity of judicial legal reasoning depends on materially higher source and authority fidelity than exploratory legal research. The reviewed evidence does not establish that Wheeler delegated authorship of the order to ChatGPT, and it does not expressly establish that a distinct required verification step was wholly omitted; VIGIL therefore does not infer Required Verification Omission as a secondary class. Fictitious-source and reliance-assurance failures are retained; the reported research use does not prove delegated authorship or complete omission of a distinct verification step. Vacatur and absence of criminal prosecution do not settle possible discipline. The safe-functioning outcome is Not aligned. The later occurrence review is Aligned for the examined material. Relevant assurance-documentation assessments remain Boundary where their decisive records are not available. Harm Impact: Fictitious AI-produced authority entered an operative paternity-case order. An attorney challenged it and the order was vacated. The meaningful bounded procedural interference and substantive remedy support S3; no lost custody right or ultimate paternity outcome is inferred.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: The occurrence demonstrates that the downstream assurance threshold is determined by the institutional use of generated or AI-assisted material. Research assistance can become governance-relevant when its outputs are incorporated into an authoritative decision without sufficient epistemic assurance, particularly where the resulting artefact can affect litigants and legal process.
assessment_boundaries: The reviewed sources report the contents of an August 17, 2026 prosecutor's letter and Wheeler's statement to investigators; VIGIL did not obtain the letter or OSBI interview record as a directly reviewed primary artefact.
The exact 2025 order date and the precise ChatGPT model/version are not established in the reviewed sources.
Wheeler reportedly stated that he created the order himself and used ChatGPT only for research; VIGIL does not characterize ChatGPT as the author of the judicial order.
The Oklahoma Attorney General's Office concluded that the evidence reviewed did not support criminal prosecution. VIGIL does not infer criminal liability or a final judicial-discipline outcome.
Other allegations investigated concerning Wheeler are outside the scope of this Incident unless independently connected to the AI-assisted citation failure.
